rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās’s account places only seven or nine jinn at Nakhlah, so crowding in the open space by the reciter makes little sense.
rows.anchor: ما ذهب إليه ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما على ما ذهب إليه المفسرون فلا معنى للازدحام إذ كان الجن بنخلة نفرا سبعة أو تسعة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They may have approached from one direction until nearly piling up; alternatively, nafar may be figurative, though that makes specifying their number pointless.
rows.anchor: حتى كادوا يكونون عليه لبدا أو بأن يتجوز في النفر

rows.speaker: ابن مسعود
rows.claim: Ibn Masʿūd places the crowd at al-Ḥajūn after returning from Nakhlah; Bursevī objects that this was witnessed, not revealed, and that few companions were with the Prophet.
rows.anchor: بطريق المشاهدة على ما أسفلناه في الأحقاف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: According to Insān al-ʿuyūn, only Zayd ibn Ḥārithah was with the Prophet, further undermining the crowding account.
rows.anchor: بل لم يكن إلا زيد ابن حارثة رضي الله عنه

words: أدعو ربي ولا أشرك به أحدا
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet worships his Lord alone; this is no novel cause for astonishment or united hostility, and others should adopt the same state.
rows.anchor: فليس ذلك ببدع فلا مستنكر يوجب التعجب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet cannot bring harm or guidance; these belong to God, with counterpart terms elided from each clause by ihtibāk.
rows.anchor: بل بيد الله تعالى فإنه هو الضار النافع الهادي المضل فترك من كلا المثقابلين

rows.speaker: القاشاني
rows.claim: Al-Qāshānī reads the trumpet’s impact as engraving harmful or saving dispositions into resurrected bodies; the day is hard for the veiled but easy for people of unveiling and vision.
rows.anchor: وقال القاشاني ينقر في البدن المبعوث فينقش فيه الهيئات السيئة المردية الموجبة للعذاب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wāḥidan can be circumstantial of the speaker—“leave me alone with him”—or of God—“I created him alone.”
rows.anchor: حال إما من الياء أي ذرني وحدي معه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With an omitted object pronoun, the phrase means the one created alone, originally without wealth or children; the verse was revealed about al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīra.
rows.anchor: أي ومن خلقته وحيدا فريدا لا مال له ولا ولد نزلت في الوليد بن المغيرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God mockingly turns al-Walīd’s title al-Waḥīd against him: he is isolated in wealthlessness or lineage as an illegitimate claimant, or uniquely evil and base.
rows.anchor: فسماه الله بالوحيد تهكما به واستهزاء بلقبه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mamdūd means abundant, extended wealth, including varied properties and produce between Mecca and Ṭāʾif.
rows.anchor: أي مبسوط أكثيرا وهو ما كان له بين مكة ولطائف

rows.speaker: النوري
rows.claim: Al-Nūrī reports that al-Walīd owned one million dinars.
rows.anchor: وقال النوري كان له ألف ألف دينار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shuhūd is the plural of shāhid, meaning present; al-Walīd’s sons were with him in Mecca.
rows.anchor: جمع شاهد مثل قاعد وقعود وشهده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their presence means either that they stayed with him for his enjoyment and were spared work by his wealth, or that they attended gatherings and enhanced his standing.
rows.anchor: أو حضورا معه في الأندية والمحافل لوجاهتهم واعتبارهم

rows.speaker: المفسرون
rows.claim: Exegetes say al-Walīd had ten sons, three of whom converted: Khālid, Hishām, and ʿAmāra.
rows.anchor: وكان له عشرة بنين أسلم منهم ثلاثة خالد وهشام وعمارة قاله المفسرون

rows.speaker: المحدثون
rows.claim: Hadith scholars say al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd converted, while ʿAmāra died an unbeliever at Badr or in Abyssinia at the Negus’s hand.
rows.anchor: وأطبق المحدثون على أن الوليد بن الوليد أسلم

rows.speaker: السهيلي
rows.claim: Al-Suhaylī names Hishām ibn al-Walīd, al-Walīd ibn al-Walīd, and Khālid ibn al-Walīd among the three; he leaves unnamed those who died in paganism.
rows.anchor: قال السهيلي رحمه الله هم هشام بن الوليد والوليد بن الوليد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God expanded al-Walīd’s leadership and prestige, completing worldly favor; worldly standards treat wealth and status together as perfection.
rows.anchor: وبسطت له الرياسة واجاه العريض فأتممت عليه النعمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Walīd was called Rayḥānat Quraysh, “Quraysh’s fragrant plant”; the passage also mentions offspring and provision.
rows.anchor: ولذا كان يلقب ريحانة قريش

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: The Najmī allusion makes al-Walīd the solitary evil soul; his wealth, bad traits, followers, and prestige symbolize sins and the dark natural powers of a rebellious self.
rows.anchor: وفي التأويلات النجمية : يشير إلى الوليد بن مغيرة

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: Abū Bakr the hidden, ʿUmar the spirit, ʿUthmān the secret, and ʿAlī the heart use spiritual light to erase the self’s darkness, defeat its deeds and followers, and end its dominion.
rows.anchor: يعني دعني وإياه فإني أسلط عليه أبا بكر الخفي وعمر الروح وعثمان السر وعلى القلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma marks distance and disapproval: hope for more is absurd after customary maximum abundance, or undeserved because he is ungrateful and defies the Benefactor.
rows.anchor: وثم استبعاد واستنكار لطمعه وحرصه إما لأنه لا مزيد على ما أوتيه سعة وكثرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bursevī also reasons that further favor will not be combined with his disbelief and ingratitude from now on.
rows.anchor: من كفران النعم ومعاندة المنعم أي لا يجمع له بعد اليوم بين الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rebukes his empty greed, cutting off his failed hope, and connects directly to what precedes.
rows.anchor: ردع وزجر له عن طمعه الفارغ وقطع لرائه الخائب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAnīd means one who knowingly opposes and rejects truth; here it is equivalent to muʿānd, like other active nouns for one who acts.
rows.anchor: يقال عند خالف الحق ورده عارفا به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fronting “Our signs” before ʿanīd restricts the enmity to those signs; this marks extreme loss despite his not opposing everything.
rows.anchor: وتقديم لآياتنا على متعلقه وهو عنيدا يدل على التخصيص

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Defying the clear Quranic signs while denying abundant favors merits total deprivation; his gifts were only gradual entrapment (istidrāj).
rows.anchor: فإن معاندة آيات المنعم وهي الآيات القرآنية مع وضوحها وكفران له مع سبوغها مما يوجب حرمانه بالكلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says al-Walīd’s wealth kept declining after revelation of this verse until he died poor.
rows.anchor: قيل ما زال بعد نزول هذه الآية في نقصان من ماله حتى هلك وهو فقير

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed Persian fragment begins by admonishing one who will not heed dear ones’ counsel; the quoted line is incomplete.
rows.anchor: آكس كه نصيحت زعزيزان نكند كوش

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He turned from truth, arrogantly refused to follow it, and then spoke.
rows.anchor: فقال} عقيب توليه عن الحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An is a negative particle meaning mā, as shown by the following illā; hādhā refers to the Quran.
rows.anchor: نافية بمعنى ما لذا أورد إلا بعدها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The charge is that magic was transmitted and learned from others, not performed by the Prophet; athara originally meant relating what one heard from predecessors, then came to mean transmitting.
rows.anchor: يقال أثرت الحديث آثهر أثرا إذا حدثت به عن قوم في آثارهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Studying magic for a sound purpose is allowed, but believing in its reality and practicing it are disbelief; the cited couplet says knowledge of evil can protect against it.
rows.anchor: وفي تعلم لسحر لحكمة رخصة واعتقاد حقيته والعمل به كفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Calling it human speech reinforces the preceding accusation; al-Walīd said it rebelliously, not sincerely, having admitted it was not human or jinn speech.
rows.anchor: تأكيد لما قبله ولذا أخرى عن العاطف

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The humans meant were Yāsār, Jabr, and Abū Fukayha: the first two were Persian slaves in Mecca whom the Prophet visited, and the third a Roman youth from Musaylima’s Yamāma.
rows.anchor: أما الأولان فكانا عبدين من بلاد فارس وكانا بمكة وكان النبي

rows.speaker: الصحاح
rows.claim: Al-Ṣiḥāḥ defines Saqar as one of the names of the Fire.
rows.anchor: لما قال في الصحاح سقر اسم من أسماء النار

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās says Saqar is Hell’s sixth level; the name is also connected to the sun burning and hurting someone.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما اسم للطبقة السادسة من جهنم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar is an inclusionary apposition for the earlier ṣaʿūd, whether hardships or a mountain of fire, since Saqar encompasses either.
rows.anchor: بدل من سأرهقه صعود أبدل الاشتمال سواء جعل مثلا لما يلقى من الشدائد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first mā is the subject with adrāka as predicate; the second describes Saqar, supplying terror and stressing its beyond-rational magnitude.
rows.anchor: ما الأولى مبتدأ وإدراك خبره وما الثانية خبر لقوله سقر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saqar burns everything cast into it, then recreates it after death to burn it again; alternatively, it spares nothing through mercy.
rows.anchor: لا تبقى شيئا يلقى فيها إلا أهلكته بالإحراق وإذا هلك لم تذره هالكا حتى يعاد خلقا جديدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A Persian glossary gives ibqāʾ the meanings preserving and showing compassion, supporting the sense that Saqar leaves no one unharmed.
rows.anchor: قال في تهذيب المصادر الإبقاء باقي كردن ونيز شفقت بردن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The creatures are described with spear-like fangs, palm-like height, red eyes, and a broad mouth that swallows people and animals; the passage links 99 dragons in the grave to disbelief in God and His 99 names, not necessarily 99 in Hell.
rows.anchor: في فمه أنياب مثل اسنة الرماح وهو طويل كالنخلة السحوق أحمر العينين مثل الدم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nine signifies domination, confinement, and extinction: mercy’s supply ceases for Hell’s inhabitants.
rows.anchor: فالتسع عدد القهر والحصر والانقراض

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: The Najmī allusion maps corruption of the human soul through deed and knowledge, and its hell of distance, expulsion, curse, and veiling, onto nine causes.
rows.anchor: ومنها ما في التأويلات النجمية : من أن اختلال النفوس البشرية بحسب العمل والعلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The nine causes are seven bodily limbs named in the prostration report plus animal nature, or anger and desire instead of nature, totaling nineteen.
rows.anchor: بقوله عليه السلام أمرت أن أسجد عى سبعة أعضاء وآراب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Aṣḥāb al-nār here are managers of Hell and punishers, unlike the phrase in 59:20; Kashf al-asrār instead supplies an omitted word for “keepers of the people of Hell,” which Bursevī calls remote.
rows.anchor: أي المدبرين لأمرها القائمين بتعذيب أهلها فأصحاب النار هنا غير أصحاب النار في قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: كشف الأسرار
rows.claim: Kashf al-asrār reads an omitted muḍāf, “keepers of the people of the Fire”; Bursevī objects that the angels keep the Fire, not its people.
rows.anchor: وفي كشف الأسرار وما جعلنا خزنة أصحاب النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The keepers are angels, unlike the humans and jinn they punish, so they do not pity them; angels are exceptionally strong and resolute in enforcing God’s command.
rows.anchor: ليخالفوا جنس المعذبين من الثقلين فلا يرقوا لهم ولا يميلوا إليهم

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying each angel’s strength equals that of both heavy species; one can drive a community into the Fire with a mountain on his neck and cast it over them.
rows.anchor: وعن النبي عليه السلام لقوة أحدهم مثل قوة الثقلين يسوق أحدهم الأمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Abū Jahl challenged Quraysh to overpower the keepers when the nineteen was revealed; Abū al-Aswad claimed he could handle seventeen if they dealt with two.
rows.anchor: ويروى إنه لما نزل قوله تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو الأسود ابن أسيد بن كلدة
rows.claim: Abū al-Aswad boasted he could resist seventeen angels, after groups failed to pull his feet off a hide without tearing it.
rows.anchor: أنا أكفيكم سبعة عشر منهم فاكفوني أنتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The different species means human messengers are sent from our kind to show mercy, while angels are the strongest creatures and most resolute in God’s right.
rows.anchor: فلذا بعث الرسول من جنسنا ليرحم بنا ولأنهم أقوى الخلق وأقومهم بحق الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nineteen is called a fitna because it causes unbelievers to stumble into disbelief; the effect is named for its cause to show their inseparability.
rows.anchor: وما جعلنا عددهم إلا العدد الذي تسبب لافتتانهم ووقوعهم في الكفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Since jaʿala takes subject and predicate, its second object must match the first; the unbelievers’ being tempted cannot literally be the number, hence the causal reading.
rows.anchor: لأن جعل من دواخل المبتدأ والخبر فوجب حمل مفعوله الثاني على الأول

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The trial is not just the angels’ actual number: stating nineteen in the Quran prompts mockery at its smallness against a vast host and sets up the following effects.
rows.anchor: بل جعله في القرآن أيضا كذلك وهو الحكم بأن عليها تسعة عشر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The purpose clause attaches to “making” in the causal sense, and the sīn indicates seeking to attain certainty.
rows.anchor: متعلق بالجعل على المعنى المذكور والسين للطلب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Scripture recipients become certain of the Prophet’s mission and the Quran’s truth by seeing it agree with their scripture.
rows.anchor: ليكتسبوا اليقين بنبوته عليه السلام وصدق القرآن لما شاهدوا ما فيه موافقا لما في كتابهم

rows.speaker: عين المعاني
rows.claim: ʿAyn al-maʿānī says Jews asked the Prophet about Hell’s keepers and their number, and he replied that there were nineteen.
rows.anchor: وفي عين المعاني سأل اليهود رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم عن خزنة النار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Believers increase in faith’s quality by seeing the People of the Book affirm the number, or in quantity by adding this belief to belief in the rest of revelation.
rows.anchor: أي بزداد إيمانهم كيفية بما رأوا من تسليم أهل الكتاب وتصديقهم إنه كذلك

words: ولا يرتاب الذين أوتوا الكتاب والمؤمنون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Denying doubt after affirming certainty and increased faith intensifies the affirmation and prevents later misgivings from weakening conviction.
rows.anchor: تأكيد لما قبله من الاستيقان وازدياد الإيمان فإن نفي ضد الشيء بعد إثبات وقوعه

words: ولا يرتاب الذين أوتوا الكتاب والمؤمنون
rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The groups’ lack of doubt accompanies different states: denial for the People of the Book, faith for believers; the active participle signals the believers’ constancy.
rows.anchor: فإن انتفاء الارتياب من أهل الكتاب مقارن لما ينافيه من الجحود

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The heart’s disease means doubt or hypocrisy; this predicts Medinan hypocrites after the Hijra, since Meccans had been believers, deniers, or doubters.
rows.anchor: شك أو نفاق فإن كلا منهما من الأمراض الباطنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbelievers are those who persist in denial.
rows.anchor: المصرون على التكذيب فإن قلت كيف يجوز أن يكون قولهم هذا مقصود الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām is consequential rather than a true purpose marker, resolving how God could intend their objectionable speech.
rows.anchor: اللام ليست على حقيقتها بل للعاقبة فلا إشكال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mathalan parses either as a specification of hādhā or its circumstantial accusative, meaning “as an example.”
rows.anchor: تمييز لهذا أو حال منه بمعنى ممثلا به كقوله هذه ناقة الله لكم آية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They metaphorically call the strange nineteen an “example,” like an oddly incomplete proverb rather than a round number; their question rejects divine authorship on that basis.
rows.anchor: فإطلاق المثل على هذا العدد على سبيل الاستعارة حيث شبهوه بالمثل المضروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This objection is singled out for its special offensiveness although it belongs to the same trial as their other reactions.
rows.anchor: وأفراد قولهم هذا بالتعليل مع كونه من باب فتنتهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Thus” points to the preceding misguidance: God misguides Abū Jahl and companions who reject the keepers and their number.
rows.anchor: ذلك إشارة إلى ما قبله من معنى الضلال أي يضل الله من يشاء إضلاله كأبي جهل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their misguidance is not imposed against choice: on seeing the signs they turn their own choice toward error, in keeping with their pre-eternal fixed essences.
rows.anchor: لصرف اختياره إلى جنب الضلال عند مشاهدته لآيات الله الناطقة بالحق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God guides whom He wills, such as Muhammad’s Companions, as they choose guidance upon seeing the signs.
rows.anchor: هدايته كأصحاب محمد عليه السلام هدايته كائنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In reality, God guides according to pre-eternal disposition; guidance and choosing its direction are eternal states that cannot be otherwise.
rows.anchor: وحقيقته إن الله لا يهي إلا بموجب الهداية الأزلية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God’s jund are His hosts of creatures, including angels; jund means army, group, or distinct class of beings.
rows.anchor: الجنود جمع جند بالضم وهو العسكر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith states that God has hosts, including honey.
rows.anchor: وفي الحديث إن الله جنودا منها العسل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says Moses asked how many inhabitants heaven had; God answered twelve tribes, each as numerous as dust.
rows.anchor: سأل ربه عن عدد أهل السماء فقال تعالى اثنا عشر سبطا

rows.speaker: الأسرار المحمدية
rows.claim: Al-Asrār al-Muḥammadiyya says every place and corner is inhabited by creatures known only to God, citing commands to cover oneself privately and not have intercourse naked.
rows.anchor: ليس في العالم موضع بيت ولا زاوية إلا وهو معمور بما لا يعلمه إلا الله

rows.speaker: القاشاني
rows.claim: Al-Qāshānī says only God knows the hosts’ number, quantity, quality, and reality because His knowledge encompasses all essences and states.
rows.anchor: وما يعلم عدد الجنود وكميتها وكيفيتها وحقيقتها إلا هو

rows.speaker: التأويلات النجمية
rows.claim: The Najmī allusion takes “He alone” as the all-encompassing divine identity, gathering infinitely many determinations of particular names and named particulars.
rows.anchor: وفي التأويلات النجمية : إلا هويته الجامعة لجميع جنود

rows.speaker: بعض العارفين
rows.claim: Some gnostics distinguish absorbed spirits devoted to glorifying God, spirits governing human and animal bodies, and many task-specific spirits serving worldly and religious needs.
rows.anchor: قال بعض العارفين خلقت الملائكة على مراتب فأرواح ليس لهم عقل إلا تعظيم جناب الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage ranks Gabriel above Azrael, Michael above Gabriel, and Israfil above Michael.
rows.anchor: وإما مراتبهم وتفاوتهم ففيهم الأكبر والكبير فجبريل أكبر من عزرائيل

rows.speaker: بعضهم
rows.claim: Another view says the hosts arrange the upper and lower worlds rather than fight, since creation serves one another.
rows.anchor: وقال بعضهم : هذه الجنود ليست معدة للمحاربة بل هي لترتيب المملكة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Angels seek forgiveness, bring revelation and law, take souls, inspire hearts, shape and ensoul fetuses, and provide sustenance and rain; every worldly event is effected by appointed angels under angelic governors.
rows.anchor: المستغفرين لمن في الأرض ومنهم الموكلون بإيصال الشرائع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ordinary people see angels’ stations as celestial bodies, not the angels themselves; people of unveiling witness angels directly at their stations.
rows.anchor: ثم إن العامة ما تشهد من هؤلاء الملائكة إلا منازلهم التي هي أجرام الكواكب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earthly rulers parallel heavenly rulers; refined correspondences reach them according to preparedness, yielding a just ruler from sound disposition and a tyrant from corrupt disposition, for which they must blame themselves.
rows.anchor: ثم اعلم أن الله قد جعل في هذا العالم العنصري خلقا من جنسهم ولاة عليهم نظير العالم العلوي

rows.speaker: الإمام الشعراني
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿrānī’s Jawāhir says subjects are beyond counting; some angels on earth never ascend and some in heaven never descend, each knowing its prayer and glorification through God’s inspiration.
rows.anchor: ولله تعالى في الأرض ملائكة لا يصعدون إلى السماء أبدا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun refers to Saqar, whose description warns people of disbelief’s end; humans are singled out because they are the primary addressees, though jinn are also warned.
rows.anchor: إلا تذكرة وعظة وإنذار لهم بسوء عاقبة الكفر والضلال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, it means the keepers’ number: God can punish an uncountable multitude with few angels and needs no helpers; assigning number and hosts reflects wisdom, not need.
rows.anchor: ليتذكروا ويعلموا أن الله قادر على أن يعذب الكثير الغير المحصور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God needs no helpers: turning one hair in the eye or causing pain in one vein would suffice as torment; He appoints hosts for a purpose.
rows.anchor: فإنه لو قلب شعرة واحدة في عين ابن آدم أو سلط الألم على عرق واحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further possibility is that the pronoun refers to the verses describing Saqar, which remind people because they contain a warning.
rows.anchor: ويجوز أن يعود الضمير إلى الآيات الناطقة بأحوال سقر فإنها تذكرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Kallā rebukes deniers of Saqar because it is real; alternatively, it denies that the people have no reminder, since failure to remember is their choice.
rows.anchor: كلا} ردع لمن أنكر سقر أي رتدع عن أنكارها فإنها حق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The next verse’s wāw is an oath particle governing the moon; the Persian gloss says knowledge of times and lifespans is tied to it.
rows.anchor: مقسم به مجرور بواو القسم يعني وسوكند بماه كه معرفت أوقات وآجال بوى باز بسته است

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An unattributed Persian couplet warns that at Israfil’s trumpet blast outward beauty will be hidden and ugly character revealed.
rows.anchor: باش نا ز صدمه صور سرافيلى شود صورت خوبت نهان وسيرت زشت آشكار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A person is a witness against himself through his limbs and accepted testimony, even if he offers every excuse: denial, motives, inability, poverty, fear, or hope of reward.
rows.anchor: أي هو بصيرة على نفسه تشهد عليه جوارحه وتقبل شهادتها ولو جاء بكل معذرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Every excuse for defending one’s deeds is useless on the day truth appears in its reality.
rows.anchor: أو ينبأ بأعماله ولو اعتذر بكل عذر في الذب عنها فإن الذب والدفع لا رواج له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Maʿādhīr is a collective plural for excuse or a plural of miʿdhār, a Yemeni word for curtain; worldly concealment cannot hide sin from oneself or the recording angels.
rows.anchor: وقيل : جمع معذار وهو الستر بلغة أهل اليمن

rows.speaker: الكشاف
rows.claim: Al-Kashshāf compares an excuse’s inability to prevent punishment with a curtain’s inability to hide the person behind it.
rows.anchor: لأنه يمنع رؤية المحتجب كما تمنع المعذرة عقوبة المذنب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: While Gabriel recites and conveys the Quran, the Prophet should not move his tongue in haste to grasp it for fear it will slip away.
rows.anchor: ما دام جبيل يقرأ ويلقى عليك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God promises to gather the Quran securely in the Prophet’s breast, so no meaning escapes; this also means establishing recitation on his tongue for later use.
rows.anchor: في صدرك بحكم الوعد بحيث لا يخفى عليك شيء من معانيه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qurʾān here is a verbal noun meaning recitation, like ghufrān for forgiveness; it means joining letters and words in ordered recitation, not any gathering.
rows.anchor: فالقرآن مصدر بمعنى القراءة كالغفران بمعنى المغفرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: When Gabriel has finished reciting the Quran, the majestic “We” magnifies the command to wait and listen.
rows.anchor: أي أتممنا قراءته عليك بلسان جبريل وإسناد القراءة إلى نون العظمة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet should begin reciting immediately after Gabriel finishes, without delay.
rows.anchor: أي فاشرع فيه بعد فراغ جبريل منه لا مهلة

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbās explains following the recitation as God establishing it in the Prophet’s breast and his acting upon it.
rows.anchor: وقال ابن عباس رضي الله عنهما ، فإذا جمعناه وأثبتناه في صدرك فاعمل به

rows.speaker: الواسطي
rows.claim: Al-Wāsiṭī reads gathering the Quran as inward and recitation as outward.
rows.anchor: وقال الواسطي رحمه الله جمعه في السر وقرآنه في العلانية

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bayān means explaining unclear Quranic meanings and rulings, revealing the intended sense of general or ambiguous wording.
rows.anchor: أي بيان ما أشكل عليك من معانيه وأحكامه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Thumma allows explanation after the address but not after the time when action is required, since that would impose an impossible obligation.
rows.anchor: وفي ثم دليل على إنه يجوز تأخر البيان عن وقت الخطاب

rows.speaker: أهل التفسير
rows.claim: Exegetes say the Prophet recited along with Gabriel before he finished, eager to memorize and fearing he would forget; he was told to listen with heart and ear until revelation ended.
rows.anchor: قال أهل التفسير كان عليه السلام إذا لقن الوحي نازع جبريل القراءة ولم يصبر
